dmm-2017-power-01.title: Pigeonhole on one person
dmm-2017-power-01.body:
Call the people $A,B,C,D,E,F$. Person $A$ has $5$ relationships with the others, each friend or stranger, so by pigeonhole $A$ has at least $3$ friends or at least $3$ strangers. Suppose $A$ has $3$ friends $B,C,D$ (the other case is identical with the roles of friends and strangers exchanged).

If two of $B,C,D$ are friends, say $B,C$, then $A,B,C$ are three mutual friends. Otherwise no two of $B,C,D$ are friends, so $B,C,D$ are three people no two of whom are friends. In either case the claim holds. ∎

dmm-2017-power-02.title: Red edges determine the coloring
dmm-2017-power-02.body: Send a coloring $c$ to the subgraph $f(c)=(V,\{e\in E_K: c(e)=\text{red}\})$. This map is surjective: given a subgraph $(V,E')$, color the edges of $E'$ red and all other edges of $K_n$ blue; this coloring maps to $(V,E')$. It is injective: if $f(c_1)=f(c_2)$ the two colorings have the same red edges, and every other edge is blue in both, so $c_1=c_2$. Hence $f$ is a bijection. ∎

dmm-2017-power-03a.title: Two inequalities
dmm-2017-power-03a.body:
*Upper bound.* Take any red-blue coloring of $K_s$. If some edge is red, it is a red $K_2$. Otherwise all edges are blue and the whole graph is a blue $K_s$. So $R(2,s)\le s$.

*Lower bound.* Color every edge of $K_{s-1}$ blue. It has no red edge, hence no red $K_2$, and it has only $s-1$ vertices so no $K_s$ at all. So $R(2,s)>s-1$. Hence $R(2,s)=s$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-03b.title: Swap the colors
dmm-2017-power-03b.body:
For a coloring $c$ let $\bar c$ be the coloring with the colors exchanged; $c\mapsto\bar c$ is a bijection on colorings of any $K_n$. A coloring $c$ of $K_n$ contains a red $K_s$ or a blue $K_t$ if and only if $\bar c$ contains a blue $K_s$ or a red $K_t$.

If every coloring of $K_n$ has a red $K_s$ or blue $K_t$, then every coloring $\bar c$ has a red $K_t$ or a blue $K_s$, and as $c$ ranges over all colorings so does $\bar c$. Thus $n\ge R(s,t)$ implies $n\ge R(t,s)$, i.e. $R(t,s)\le R(s,t)$. Exchanging the roles of $s$ and $t$ gives the reverse inequality, so $R(s,t)=R(t,s)$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-04a.title: Pentagon and pentagram
dmm-2017-power-04a.body:
Label the vertices $v_1,\dots,v_5$ around a pentagon. Color the five sides $v_iv_{i+1}$ (indices mod $5$) red and the five diagonals $v_iv_{i+2}$ blue.

A red triangle would need three vertices pairwise adjacent on the pentagon, but the pentagon (a $5$-cycle) has no triangle. A blue triangle would need three vertices pairwise at distance $2$ around the cycle, but the diagonals also form a $5$-cycle $v_1v_3v_5v_2v_4$, which has no triangle. So there is no monochromatic $K_3$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-04b.title: Combine two facts
dmm-2017-power-04b.body: Every coloring of $K_6$ contains a monochromatic $K_3$ (the six-people party problem), so $R(3,3)\le6$. The coloring of $K_5$ with no monochromatic triangle (pentagon red, pentagram blue) shows $R(3,3)>5$. Hence $R(3,3)=6$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-05a.title: Restrict to a subgraph
dmm-2017-power-05a.body: Let $n=R(s,t)\le N$. Pick any $n$ vertices of $K_N$; they span a copy of $K_n$. The given coloring restricted to it is a red-blue coloring of $K_n$, so by the definition of $R(s,t)$ it contains a red $K_s$ or a blue $K_t$, which is also contained in $K_N$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-05b.title: Pigeonhole at one vertex
dmm-2017-power-05b.body:
Let $N=R(s-1,t)+R(s,t-1)$ and color $K_N$. Fix a vertex $A$; it has $N-1=R(s-1,t)+R(s,t-1)-1$ edges, so it has at least $R(s-1,t)$ red edges or at least $R(s,t-1)$ blue edges.

*Case 1: at least $R(s-1,t)$ red edges.* Their other endpoints span a $K_{R(s-1,t)}$ (or larger), which contains a red $K_{s-1}$ or a blue $K_t$. A blue $K_t$ is what we want; a red $K_{s-1}$ together with $A$ (joined to it by red edges) forms a red $K_s$.

*Case 2: at least $R(s,t-1)$ blue edges.* Symmetrically we get a red $K_s$, or a blue $K_{t-1}$ which together with $A$ gives a blue $K_t$.

In every case there is a red $K_s$ or a blue $K_t$, so $R(s,t)\le N$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-05c.title: Induction on $s+t$
dmm-2017-power-05c.body: Note $R(1,t)=R(s,1)=1$ (a single vertex is already a $K_1$ of either color), and $R(2,t)=t$, $R(s,2)=s$ are finite. Induct on $s+t$. The base cases are those with $\min(s,t)\le2$. If $s,t\ge3$ and all Ramsey numbers with smaller $s+t$ are finite, then $R(s-1,t)$ and $R(s,t-1)$ are finite, so by the previous inequality $R(s,t)\le R(s-1,t)+R(s,t-1)<\infty$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-05d.title: Induction with Pascal's rule
dmm-2017-power-05d.body:
Induct on $s+t$. If $s=2$ then $R(2,t)=t=\binom{t}{1}$, and if $t=2$ then $R(s,2)=s=\binom{s}{s-1}$, so the bound holds (with equality). For $s,t\ge3$, using the recursive inequality and the induction hypothesis,
$$R(s,t)\le R(s-1,t)+R(s,t-1)\le\binom{s+t-3}{s-2}+\binom{s+t-3}{s-1}=\binom{s+t-2}{s-1}$$
by Pascal's rule. ∎

dmm-2017-power-05e.title: Compare with the binomial sum
dmm-2017-power-05e.body: By the previous bound $R(s,s)\le\binom{2s-2}{s-1}$. This is one term of the binomial expansion $\sum_{k}\binom{2s-2}{k}=2^{2s-2}$, so $\binom{2s-2}{s-1}\le2^{2s-2}$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-06a.title: The circulant coloring
dmm-2017-power-06a.body:
Let $N=3s-1$ and use the vertices $\mathbb Z_N$. Color the edge $\{i,j\}$ red if $i-j\equiv s,s+1,\dots,2s-1\pmod N$ (this set is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$, since $N-(2s-1)=s$), and blue otherwise, i.e. when the circular distance of $i,j$ is at most $s-1$. (For $s=3$, $N=8$, the red edges join vertices at distance $3$ or $4$, which is the picture.)

*No red triangle.* If $i,j,k$ were pairwise red, the three differences $j-i,\ k-j,\ i-k$ (taken as residues in $[s,2s-1]$) would add up to a multiple of $N$. Their sum lies in $[3s,\,6s-3]$, but the multiples of $N=3s-1$ near this range are $3s-1<3s$ and $2N=6s-2>6s-3$. So no red triangle.

*No blue $K_{s+1}$.* Suppose $K$ is a set of $s+1$ vertices with pairwise circular distance at most $m=s-1$. Pick $x\in K$. Every other point lies in $[x-m,x+m]$. If there are points $y$ to the left of $x$ and $z$ to the right, the distance from $y$ to $z$ going through $x$ is at most $2m$, so going the other way it is at least $N-2m=s+1>m$; hence the circular distance of $y,z$ must be the one through $x$, so it is $\le m$. It follows that all of $K$ lies in an arc of at most $m+1=s$ consecutive vertices (if all other points are on one side of $x$ this is clear too). But $|K|=s+1>s$, a contradiction.

So this coloring of $K_{3s-1}$ has no red $K_3$ and no blue $K_{s+1}$, hence $R(3,s+1)>3s-1$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-06b.title: Degree count in $K_9$
dmm-2017-power-06b.body:
The lower bound $R(3,4)>8$ is part (a) with $s=3$. For the upper bound, suppose a red-blue coloring of $K_9$ has no red $K_3$ and no blue $K_4$.

*Red degree $\le3$.* If a vertex $v$ had $4$ red neighbours, then no two of them can be joined by a red edge (a red triangle), so all $6$ edges among them are blue and they form a blue $K_4$.

*Blue degree $\le5$.* If $v$ had $6$ blue neighbours, then among those $6$ vertices there is a monochromatic triangle. It cannot be red, so it is blue, and together with $v$ it gives a blue $K_4$.

Every vertex has degree $8=\text{red}+\text{blue}\le3+5$, so every vertex has red degree exactly $3$. Then the number of red edges is $\frac{9\cdot3}{2}=13.5$, which is not an integer, a contradiction. Hence $R(3,4)\le9$, and $R(3,4)=9$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-07.title: Both bounds
dmm-2017-power-07.body:
*Upper bound.* $R(4,4)\le R(3,4)+R(4,3)=9+9=18$.

*Lower bound.* Let $S=\{1,2,4,8,9,13,15,16\}=\{\pm1,\pm2,\pm4,\pm8\}$, the set of nonzero squares mod $17$ ($1,4,9,16,8,2,15,13$). A product of two elements of $S$ is in $S$, and a nonzero residue times a non-square is a non-square. Let $N$ be the $8$ non-squares.

*No red $K_4$.* Suppose $\{a,b,c,d\}$ is a red $K_4$. Translating, assume $a=0$; then $b,c,d\in S$. Multiplying everything by $b^{-1}\in S$ preserves $S$ and differences, so we may assume $b=1$. Then $c,d\in S$ with $c-1,d-1\in S$: checking the elements of $S$, $c-1\in S$ only for $c\in\{2,9,16\}$ (since $2-1=1$, $9-1=8$, $16-1=15$). Among $2,9,16$ the differences $9-2=7$, $16-2=14$, $16-9=7$ are not in $S$, so $c,d$ cannot both exist. No red $K_4$.

*No blue $K_4$.* Multiplication by $3$ (a non-square) maps $S$ to $N$ and vice versa, so it maps red edges to blue edges and blue to red. A blue $K_4$ would map to a red $K_4$, which does not exist.

So this coloring of $K_{17}$ has no monochromatic $K_4$, hence $R(4,4)>17$. Together with the upper bound, $R(4,4)=18$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-08a.title: Merge two colors
dmm-2017-power-08a.body: Let $n=R_{r-1}(R(s_1,s_2),s_3,\dots,s_r)$ and take any $r$-coloring of $K_n$. Regard colors $1$ and $2$ as a single color; this is an $(r-1)$-coloring, so it contains either a $K_{s_i}$ of color $i$ for some $i\ge3$ (and we are done), or a $K_{R(s_1,s_2)}$ using only colors $1$ and $2$. In the latter case, by the definition of $R(s_1,s_2)$, that subgraph contains a $K_{s_1}$ of color $1$ or a $K_{s_2}$ of color $2$. In all cases an $r$-colored $K_n$ has a $K_{s_j}$ of color $j$ for some $j$, so $R_r(s_1,\dots,s_r)\le n$. ∎

dmm-2017-power-08b.title: Use the merging inequality
dmm-2017-power-08b.body:
By the merging inequality, $R_3(3,3,3)\le R_2(R(3,3),3)=R(6,3)$, since $R(3,3)=6$. By the bound $R(s,t)\le\binom{s+t-2}{s-1}$, $R(6,3)\le\binom{7}{5}=21$. So $R_3(3,3,3)\le21$. (The true value is $17$.)

**Answer: $R_3(3,3,3)\le21$**
